title: His students
hookLine: Abu Yusuf and Muhammad al-Shaybani spread the school

cards: In the classic Hanafi law books, a strange habit shows up again and again. A ruling is given, and then: Abu Hanifa said this, but Abu Yusuf and Muhammad said that.
The founder, contradicted by his own students, on the same page of the school's own book. Nobody tore the page out. Nobody threw the students out.
Their names sit beside his, and sometimes later Hanafi scholars even follow the students' view over the teacher's. An odd way to honor a teacher, until you see what the students were doing.

teach.h: ABU YUSUF: THE JUDGE AT COURT.
teach.b: The first is Abu Yusuf. He sat in Abu Hanifa's circle in Kufa and later served as a judge for the Abbasid caliphs.
For the caliph Harun al-Rashid he wrote Kitab al-Kharaj, a book on taxes and the public treasury, giving the school's reasoning a place at court.

The second is Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Shaybani, the great writer of the pair. His books set down the school's positions in order, and Hanafi scholars came to treat a set of them as the school's core record.
They say much of Abu Hanifa's teaching reached later readers through what these two wrote.

teach.h: THE TWO COMPANIONS DISAGREE ON THE PAGE.
teach.b: Hanafi books call the three the imams of the school, and the students the two companions. When the companions disagreed with their teacher, they said so, and the books kept every view.
For a school built on reasoned judgment, that fits. A student who repeats a teacher's answers carries the answers.

teach.h: A WEEK OF METHOD, CARRIED ON.
teach.b: A student who learned the method can carry the method, even past the teacher.
So the week closes: most of life simply permitted, ijtihad, taqlid, difference as mercy, Abu Hanifa and his ra'y, and now the people who made sure any of it survived. A school isn't one man.
It's a teacher, and students honest enough to argue with him, and to write it all down.

how: Hanafi law books record the views of Abu Hanifa beside those of his students Abu Yusuf and Muhammad al-Shaybani, and later Hanafi jurists weigh all three when deciding the school's position.

o: Abu Hanifa's sons, who took over his cloth trade
Malik and al-Shafi'i, who studied in his circle in Kufa
Abu Yusuf and al-Shaybani, who wrote the Hanafi school down

p: a book on taxes, for Harun al-Rashid

s: Hanafi books only record Abu Hanifa's own view
they keep his students' views beside his, even where they disagree.
much of what is known of Abu Hanifa's teaching comes through his students' writing
al-Shaybani in particular set the school's positions down.
a student who disagreed with Abu Hanifa left the school
the two companions disagreed often and are still called imams of the school.

games.q: you're a student of Abu Hanifa, and on one question you've reached a different answer than his. what does the school do with your view?
o: strike it out, out of respect for the teacher.
record it beside his, by name.
keep it secret until he dies.
games.why: the books say Abu Hanifa held this, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad held that, and sometimes later jurists follow the students.

practice: Bring to mind someone who learned something from you: a younger sibling you taught to ride a bike, a new colleague, a child who now makes a recipe your way, or better than your way.
Hold their face for a moment and notice what they kept, what they changed, and where they disagree with you now. If you pray, you can remember them in your prayer.

wordCard.voice: His students. Abu Yusuf and Muhammad al-Shaybani, the two companions, who wrote the Hanafi school down and spread it, keeping their own views beside their teacher's. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: students, pupils; the Hanafi books also call the two the sahiban, the two companions.

carryVoice: Your line: students carry it. The method can travel even past the teacher. That's today, done.

sources.ref: Muhammad al-Shaybani, the books of zahir al-riwayah (e.g. al-Asl, al-Jami' al-Saghir)
